title: Tenant late-response communication playbook and post-incident note
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a customer-facing communications playbook and a draft post-incident note for a class of incidents we observed where tenant requests experienced unexpectedly long tail response times ("late responses"). It is intended for rapid status-page posts, enterprise account email templates, and a short postmortem summary aimed at product teams and engineering leads at affected customers.

Executive summary (for status page snippet):
Between 2029-06-30 02:14 UTC and 2029-06-30 05:03 UTC, a subset of requests routed to Redwood’s hosted inference service experienced intermittent long-tail response times (requests taking 10s–60s). The issue affected ~3% of traffic for impacted regions and specific tenants with high-concurrency, long-sequence workloads. We implemented progressive routing and cache-priming mitigations and fully restored normal latency by 05:03 UTC. No customer data was lost and model outputs remain intact.

Severity classification:
- Impact: degraded latency for a subset of tenants; some streaming sessions timed out or were retried by customers.
- Scope: multi-region but concentrated on eu-west and us-central clusters with mixed CPU/GPU routing.
- Duration: ~2h49m total window of elevated tail latency; degraded window for some customers extended slightly due to client retries.

What we told customers (status page language — short):
We identified elevated tail latency affecting some requests to our hosted API. Engineers have implemented automated routing adjustments and temporary capacity increases; metric signals now show return to normal. For customers still seeing issues, please retry requests or contact your account lead. A technical summary will follow.

Detailed customer post-incident note (draft):
Root cause (high level):
A subtle interaction between our request router’s backpressure heuristics and our long-sequence KV-cache warm paths caused a small subset of requests to be assigned to nodes that were momentarily saturated for KV cache population. Because those requests carried long input sequences and enabled streaming, the per-token processing time spiked for those sessions until the cache fully populated. Simultaneously, our routing fallback delay threshold (intended to avoid flapping) was set conservatively for these clusters, delaying automatic re-routing for ~20–40s in affected flows.

Contributing factors:
- Increased concentration of long-sequence, multi-turn chat traffic from a few high-concurrency tenants.
- Recently rolled kernel selection change in eu-west that altered memory prefetch behavior (rollout 2029-06-29).
- Conservative fallback timer in the smart-router configuration that extends re-routing decisions.

Impact summary for customers:
- Some API calls experienced significantly higher latency (10s–60s).
- Affected customers saw increased timeouts and some duplicated retries.
- No model outputs were corrupted; ordering and integrity checks passed.
- No PII or customer content was exposed. Logs and request payloads were retained per standard retention policy.

Mitigation and recovery steps we performed:
1) Immediately increased routing margin for affected clusters to allow more aggressive re-routing of heavy sequences.
2) Deployed a targeted rollback of the kernel-prefetch tweak to eu-west for older hardware profiles.
3) Temporarily increased capacity for dedicated job queues (reservations + burst pools) and enabled short-lived warm-up workers to populate KV caches faster.
4) Adjusted monitoring thresholds to surface similar tail-latency patterns earlier.
These actions collectively reduced the tail and returned the metric curves to baseline by 05:03 UTC.

Customer-facing recommendations (what customers can do now):
- If you observed timeouts, please retry the request once; our platform will have reduced the tail risk.
- For mission-critical streaming flows, consider enabling the platform's "fast-fail fallback" (document link) which routes streaming attempts to an alternate model variant with similar semantics and lower cold-cache cost.
- If your workload has frequent long sequences, contact Solutions Engineering for guidance on batching/caching configuration and tokenization settings that reduce cache population latency.

Operational follow-ups (action items we will share):
- Short-term (next 72h): revert fallback timer from conservative to adaptive mode for EU/US clusters; add a canary for the kernel-prefetch change; increase warm-up worker ratio.
- Medium-term (2–4 weeks): build per-tenant sequence-profiled routing (route heavy-sequence tenants to pre-warmed nodes), extend kv-cache prefetch heuristics, and improve observability to correlate sequence length distributions with tail-latency.
- Postmortem deliverable: a technical root-cause analysis and a public postmortem note with timeline, and a customer-facing FAQ will be published to the incident page.

Compensation & SLAs:
We recognize the operational impact for affected tenants. For customers on committed Dedicated plans or enterprise contracts who experienced SLA breaches during this window, CS will open SLA credit requests per contract terms. If you want us to initiate this on your behalf, reply to this notice or contact your account manager.

Customer Q&A (short FAQ):
Q: Was data lost or changed?
A: No. Requests completed either succeeded or timed out; outputs were not altered and request logs remain intact.

Q: Will this recur after the kernel-prefetch rollback?
A: Temporarily reducing the aggressiveness of the prefetch reduces risk; we are also implementing routing improvements to lower recurrence probability. The kernel tweak will be reintroduced to canaries after additional telemetry.

Q: Are private deployments affected?
A: Private deployments and VPC installations are not directly affected by this hosted incident unless you share our hosted routing/prefetch configuration. Customers with Private deployments should consult release notes if they recently applied the kernel-prefetch change.

Draft email template for enterprise contacts (short):
Subject: Incident summary — elevated tail latency 2029-06-30 (tenant classes)
Hi <CustomerLead>,
We wanted to make you aware of an incident on 2029-06-30 that caused elevated response times for a subset of requests. Engineers have implemented mitigations and full recovery was confirmed at 05:03 UTC. We do not identify data loss or corruption. We will follow up with a technical summary and action timeline; if you saw customer impact, we can open an SLA review on your behalf.
Regards,
Aisha (on behalf of CS & SRE)

Notes to internal teams / optional attachments for enterprise packet:
- Metric snapshots (tail p95/p99), trace examples, affected tenant list (internal-only), timelines with bounded request IDs, and suggested tokenization/batch settings.
- Link to incident dashboard and temporary canary config: https://status.redwood.example/incident/INC-2029-06-30-42

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we want to proactively notify all tenants with long-sequence traffic patterns or only those showing retries/timeouts? Recommendation: notify any tenant with >1% requests failing/timeouting during window.
- Post-rollback, schedule reintroduce of the kernel change behind an adaptive canary? Recommendation: yes, but gated on new metrics.

Appendix — quick recovery timeline (UTC):
- 02:14: alerting fired (elevated p99 tokens)
- 02:22: first customer-facing status page notice posted
- 02:35: routing margin increased; additional warm-up workers provision started
- 03:05: kernel-prefetch rollback began to eu-west older nodes
- 04:10: fallback timer adjusted to adaptive mode in us-central and eu-west
- 05:03: p99 metrics returned to baseline; incident declared resolved

If you have edits or prefer different wording for your enterprise outreach, leave comments here and CS will coordinate with SRE/product to finalize the public postmortem.
